concepts.title: Endogenetic and Exogenetic Forces and Diastrophism
concepts.definition: The earth's surface is shaped by endogenetic forces of diastrophism and volcanism acting from within, and exogenetic forces of weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition acting from outside, and the balance of the two keeps the surface in perpetual change.
concepts.key_idea: Diastrophism includes folding, faulting and warping of the crust, while sudden endogenetic movements cause earthquakes and volcanoes.

concepts.title: Weathering, Mass Movements and Erosion-Deposition
concepts.definition: Weathering is the in-situ breaking of rocks by chemical, physical and biological processes, mass movements transport weathered material downslope under gravity, and erosion by running water, wind, glaciers and waves removes and deposits material across the surface.
concepts.key_idea: Chemical weathering processes include solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction, while physical weathering uses unloading, thermal expansion and freeze-thaw.

concepts.title: Evolution of Landforms and Significance for Humans
concepts.definition: Landform evolution proceeds from youth to old age under each geomorphic agent, and the resulting plains, valleys and slopes decide soils, water supply, settlement and farming, so geomorphic knowledge guides land use and hazard avoidance.
concepts.key_idea: Slope stability, floodplain siting and groundwater recharge all depend on reading the geomorphic history of a landscape.
